title: Measurement Types
text:
Gain (similar to voltage on certain cytometers) is an unit which detected signal is amplified by for each detector. An instrument applies different gains to each detector, allowing for use of dim and bright fluorophores. During the Daily QC, these gains normally get minor adjustments to keep the QC beads’ signal constant, allowing for comparison of .fcs files acquired on different days. As the individual lasers in the cytometer are used, they slowly wear down and more gain is applied to remain at that setpoint. This contributes to the slowly increasing view typical of the gain plots:





Generally, when a laser is begining to rapidly wear out, we see steeper increases in the Gain plots. When the field service engineer replaces the laser, the gain values are reset according to the new laser. In this example, you can see that pattern for the violet laser of the instrument was replaced twice (red lines indicating field service engineer visit):





For the Cytek instruments, a Daily QC fail is triggered when the Gain is >100% of the original baseline Gain value. When this happens, a red flag is added to that timepoint. We have observed that .fcs files acquired on gain spike days (as seen below) may still have altered unmixing even if they have not exceeded the >100% threshold, so it’s worth keeping an eye on.








The robust coefficient of variation (rCV) is a measure of the resolution between the positive and negative population for each detector. When the value is high, dim staining populations may be harder to distinguish from the negative population. For spectral instruments where entire spectrum is used to identify a fluorophore, increased rCV on the detector where a fluorophore has its main peak has impacted unmixing for users with larger panels (>20 fluorophores). The RCV plots will typically resemble the following:





For Cytek instruments, a Daily QC fail is only triggered when %rCV exceeds either 8% for SSC, or 6% for FSC and the following detectors: UV3, V3, B3, YG3, R3. When this happens, the instrument will appear as failed on the home page:





When we navigate to the History tab and find that date, we can see that the rCV for UV3 failed, which was what triggered the QC fail:





But what happens if the RCV fails on any of the other detectors (UV1-> UV2, UV4 -> UV16,etc.)? Since they are not the indicator detectors, they won’t trigger a Cytek QC fail. However, since we have observed unmixing issues when the RCVs of these other detectors are exceeded, we don’t want to ignore them. Consequently, when a non-indicator RCV fails, we show it as failed under the Daily View:





And label the instrument as caution for that given day:





How to interpret these Caution notices depends on what we see in the Levey-Jennings plots. For a few detectors (especially UV1/UV2), they exceed the 6% cutoff but are stable over time. Consequently, the impact of the increased RCV is relatively minimal.





By contrast, is the RCV went from consistently stable, to spiking, the impact on your unmixing is likely to be significantly greater.

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text: Secondary QC for the Cytek Aurora EVO from SPHERO URCP-38-2K Ultra Rainbow beads. The set resolves into 6 populations — blank particles (peak 1) plus 5 fluorescent rainbow levels (peaks 2–6). Note on the Aurora: daily QC adjusts each APD’s gain to pin bead MFI to a target, so raw MFI is held ~constant by design — the informative signals are the ones gain can’t compensate: sensitivity (Q & B), resolution, %CV, linearity, and spectral-signature stability. Heavy FCS processing is done once by scripts/Process6PeakUltra.R; this page reads the peak_metrics.csv archive (+ the daily-QC gain) so it stays light.

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Sensitivity (Q & B)
Q = detection efficiency (photoelectrons per unit signal, gain-normalised) — a drop means the detector collects less light per event. B = background/noise term; intrinsic CV = the high-signal noise floor (bead + optics). Estimated per detector from CV² vs 1/MFI across the resolved peaks. Because Q = 1/slope blows up when the slope nears zero, fits that are ill-conditioned — near-flat or negative slope, R² < 0.8, a non-monotonic CV profile, or a brightest-peak CV > 15% — are suppressed (left blank) rather than reported as a phantom Q spike; the underlying cause then shows in the %CV panel.






NoteMethod & provenance — read me





This is the Q–B detector-sensitivity model of Hoffman & Wood (Wood JC, Cytometry 1998;33:260–266; Wood & Hoffman, Cytometry 1998;33:256–259; Chase & Hoffman, Cytometry 1998;33:267–279; Hoffman & Wood, Current Protocols in Cytometry Unit 1.20, 2007), the same model behind Spherotech’s STN-17 and BD’s CS&T Qr/Br. Total spread decomposes as CV² = CV_intr² + (1/Q)(1/S) + (B/Q)(1/S²); fitting CV² vs 1/S gives intrinsic CV (intercept), 1/Q (linear term) and B/Q (curvature).
The panel-wide values use gain-normalised MFI (S = MFI/gain), not MEF, so Q and B are a relative, non-normalised index — valid for single-detector trend monitoring (Levey-Jennings), not cross-detector comparison, and expect small steps when a bead lot changes. Absolute, gain-independent sensitivity lives in the MEF-unit Q/B and detection-limit (MEF) panels below, on the anchor detectors.




Code
if (fc_locked) cat(sprintf("> **FC reference: LOCKED** to qualified window %s – %s (per-detector median ± SD).\n",
                           fc_ref_window[1], fc_ref_window[2])) else
  cat(sprintf("> **FC reference: dynamic / preliminary** — each detector vs its own best of %d run(s). Lock a fixed reference once enough qualified runs accumulate.\n", n_runs))


FC reference: dynamic / preliminary — each detector vs its own best of 4 run(s). Lock a fixed reference once enough qualified runs accumulate.


Code
gp(heat(qb, "Q", "Detection efficiency Q", "absolute — gain-normalised; higher = better"))
gp(heat_fc(qb, "Q", "Q — fold-change (per detector)", "vs its own best; red = degraded", higher_better = TRUE))

















Background B is shown absolute only: the relative B is a fit coefficient that can be ≤ 0, so a fold-change vs best is undefined for it.


Code
gp(heat(qb |> filter(is.finite(B)), "B", "Background B", "absolute — higher = more background/noise"))








Code

if (nrow(flagged)) {
  fl <- flagged |> group_by(run_label) |>
    summarise(`detectors suppressed` = n(),
              `example reasons` = paste(head(sort(unique(qflag)), 3), collapse = " | "),
              .groups = "drop")
  knitr::kable(fl, caption = "Detector-runs where the Q/B fit was suppressed as ill-conditioned (blank tiles above) — NOT a sensitivity gain. The cause appears in the %CV & noise-floor panel.")
}

ql <- qb |> mutate(laser = factor(laser_of(detector), levels = laser_levels)) |>
  group_by(laser, run_label) |> summarise(Q = median(Q, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
gp(ggplot(ql, aes(run_label, Q, colour = laser, group = laser,
                  text = sprintf("%s laser | %s<br>median Q %.3g", laser, run_label, Q))) +
     geom_line() + geom_point() +
     labs(title = "Median detection efficiency per laser over time", x = NULL, y = "Q (median)") +
     theme_bw(base_size = 10) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)), 320)






True sensitivity in standardized units — the detection limit (MEF) per anchor detector from the URCP-38-2K calibration. Gain-independent, so a rise is a real sensitivity loss (not the QC gain loop).


Code
gp(ggplot(sens, aes(run_label, MEF_LOD, colour = detector, group = detector,
                    text = sprintf("%s (%s)<br>%s<br>MEF LOD %.0f", detector, fluor, run_label, MEF_LOD))) +
     geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_y_log10() +
     labs(title = "Detection limit (MEF) per anchor detector — URCP-38-2K",
          x = NULL, y = "MEF at detection threshold (log)") +
     theme_bw(base_size = 10) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)), 340)







Q & B in MEF units (anchor detectors)
The Q/B heatmaps above are in gain-normalised MFI units — comparable across the full 64-detector panel, but arbitrary. On the anchor detectors (where the URCP-38-2K certificate gives a per-peak MEF) the same CV² regression is run against true MEF, yielding Q and B in absolute, gain-independent units matching the Spherotech STN-17 definition. The intrinsic CV (high-signal floor) is scale-invariant, so it should agree between the two fits — a built-in check.


Code
gp(ggplot(qb_mef, aes(run_label, Q, colour = detector, group = detector,
        text = sprintf("%s (%s)<br>%s<br>Q(MEF) %.3g | B(MEF) %.3g | intrinsic CV %.2f%%",
                       detector, fluor, run_label, Q, B, 100 * intr_cv))) +
     geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_y_log10() +
     labs(title = "Detection efficiency Q in MEF units — anchor detectors (STN-17)",
          x = NULL, y = "Q (MEF units, log)") +
     theme_bw(base_size = 10) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)), 340)

            `intr.CV % (MEF fit)` = round(100 * intr_cv, 2)) |>

The regression above uses every resolved peak. As an independent check, the literal STN-17 closed form uses just three populations — the blank (peak 1), the dimmest fluorescent bead carrying an assigned MEF (peak 3) and the brightest (peak 6). The blank carries no assigned MEF, so it is extrapolated through the per-run calibration, then Q = 1/(CV²_blank × MEF_blank). The two Q estimates won’t match exactly (3-point algebra vs. multi-point fit) but should track each other; large divergence flags a nonlinear detector.

text:
Resolution & SI
Number of the 6 populations resolved per detector (0–6) and the staining index (lowest resolved peak vs the blank). Detectors losing dim peaks over time = rising noise floor.

gp(heat_fc(si |> filter(is.finite(si)), "si", "Staining index — fold-change", "vs its own best; red = degraded", higher_better = TRUE))

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
%CV & noise floor
Peak 6 (brightest) uses robust %CV — it has a well-defined mean (~1–2% when healthy). The blank (peak 1) uses its absolute robust spread (IQR/1.349), not %CV: the blank sits near zero, so %CV explodes when the mean dips toward zero even though the actual spread is unchanged. A rising blank spread is a genuine noise-floor increase.

gp(heat_fc(cvp1, "sd1", "Noise floor — fold-change", "lower is better; red = noisier than its best", higher_better = FALSE))

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Gain context
The daily-QC gain applied on each run (rising = APD/laser aging) and MFI/gain (gain-removed bead intensity; should be flat if the bead + optics are stable).

Code
if (length(runs_no_gain)) cat(sprintf(
  "::: {.callout-warning appearance='simple'}\nNo daily-QC gain found in the archive for **%s** — these run(s) are shown blank on every gain-normalised panel (relative Q/B, MFI/gain, and the executive overview's Q & MFI rows) rather than mixed onto a raw-MFI scale. Their **gain-independent** metrics (MEF-unit Q/B, linearity, detection limit, resolution, %CV, spectral signature) are unaffected and fully valid. Update `data/EVO/Archive/ArchivedDataEVO.csv` with the run's gain to populate the gain panels.\n:::\n\n",
  paste(runs_no_gain, collapse = ", ")))



Code
gtab <- pm |> filter(peak == n_peaks) |> distinct(run_label, detector, gain)
gp(heat(gtab, "gain", "Applied gain (peak-7 row)", "from daily QC"))

title: 8 Peak Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text: Secondary QC for the Cytek Aurora EVO from RCP-30-5A 8-peak beads. Note on the Aurora: daily QC adjusts each APD’s gain to pin bead MFI to a target, so raw MFI is held ~constant by design — the informative signals are the ones gain can’t compensate: sensitivity (Q & B), resolution, %CV, linearity, and spectral-signature stability. Heavy FCS processing is done once by scripts/Process8Peak.R; this page reads the peak_metrics.csv archive (+ the daily-QC gain) so it stays light.

title: 8 Peak Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Sensitivity (Q & B)
Q = detection efficiency (photoelectrons per unit signal, gain-normalised) — a drop means the detector collects less light per event. B = background/noise term; intrinsic CV = the high-signal noise floor (bead + optics). Estimated per detector from CV² vs 1/MFI across the resolved peaks. Because Q = 1/slope blows up when the slope nears zero, fits that are ill-conditioned — near-flat or negative slope, R² < 0.8, a non-monotonic CV profile, or a brightest-peak CV > 15% (e.g. a laser-instability run) — are suppressed (left blank) rather than reported as a phantom Q spike; the underlying cause then shows in the %CV panel.






NoteMethod & provenance — read me





This is the Q–B detector-sensitivity model of Hoffman & Wood (Wood JC, Cytometry 1998;33:260–266; Wood & Hoffman, Cytometry 1998;33:256–259; Chase & Hoffman, Cytometry 1998;33:267–279; Hoffman & Wood, Current Protocols in Cytometry Unit 1.20, 2007), the same model behind Spherotech’s STN-17 and BD’s CS&T Qr/Br (BD app note “Qr and Br in BD FACSDiva Software”, 2012). Total spread decomposes as CV² = CV_intr² + (1/Q)(1/S) + (B/Q)(1/S²); fitting CV² vs 1/S gives intrinsic CV (intercept), 1/Q (linear term) and B/Q (curvature) — algebraically identical to BD’s SD² = (1/Q)·S + B/Q fit with Q = 1/slope, B = Q·intercept (the MEF table’s true_b), and to STN-17’s closed form.
These panel-wide values use gain-normalised MFI (S = MFI/gain), not MESF, so Q and B are a relative, non-normalised index — not absolute MESF units. This is deliberate and is the intended use: BD reports its own Qr/Br in relative ABD units, and explicitly states that non-normalised Qr “values are still valid and serve as a powerful metric for tracking changes in detector performance over time” — a 50% change in a non-normalised Qr equals a 50% change in a normalised one. So treat these for single-detector trend monitoring (Levey-Jennings), not for cross-detector or cross-instrument comparison, and expect small steps when a bead lot changes. Absolute, gain-independent sensitivity lives in the MEF-unit Q/B and detection-limit (MEF) panels below, on the anchor detectors.



Fold-change maps: beside each absolute map, a companion normalises every detector to its own reference, stripping out absolute magnitude so dim and bright detectors are directly comparable and the colour isn’t dominated by the few brightest. The reference has two modes (set by fc_ref_window in the load chunk):

Dynamic / preliminary (current): reference = each detector’s best run so far. Good while characterising, but it shifts retroactively as runs accumulate, so it can’t anchor a stable trend.
Locked: once ~8–10 qualified runs exist, set fc_ref_window to a date range of known-good runs. The per-detector robust centre (median) ± SD over that window is frozen to data/reference/EVO_8peak_reference.csv, and the maps switch to a two-sided deviation-from-qualified-normal view (red = worse, in log₂ and SD units) where real drift and control-limit breaches emerge against a fixed anchor.


Code
if (fc_locked) cat(sprintf("> **FC reference: LOCKED** to qualified window %s – %s (per-detector median ± SD). Maps show deviation from qualified normal.\n",
                           fc_ref_window[1], fc_ref_window[2])) else
  cat(sprintf("> **FC reference: dynamic / preliminary** — each detector vs its own best of %d run(s). Lock a fixed reference once enough qualified runs accumulate.\n", n_runs))

Q & B in MEF units (anchor detectors)
The Q/B heatmaps above are in gain-normalised MFI units — comparable across the full 64-detector panel, but arbitrary. On the anchor detectors (where lot AS01 gives a per-peak MEF) the same CV² regression can be run against true MEF, yielding Q and B in absolute, gain-independent units that match the Spherotech STN-17 definition. Because daily QC re-gains each detector, this MEF-anchored sensitivity is the more defensible cross-day metric: it re-anchors to the bead lot’s physical scale rather than trusting the recorded gain. The intrinsic CV (high-signal floor) is scale-invariant, so it should agree between the two fits — a built-in consistency check.

     geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_y_log10() +
     labs(title = "Detection efficiency Q in MEF units — anchor detectors (STN-17)",
          x = NULL, y = "Q (MEF units, log)") +
     theme_bw(base_size = 10), 340)

Peak 8 (brightest) uses robust %CV — it has a well-defined mean (~1–2% when healthy).
